abstract: Deleting a thin set $S$ of rational primes of convergence exponent $\alpha\in(1/2,1)$ gives a Beurling system whose primes violate the square-root law with exponent $\alpha$ under RH. A companion paper (rStation riemann_hypothesis_116) showed that, under RH, random sifting reaches integer error $x^{\alpha/2+\varepsilon}$ when $\alpha\le2/3$, and that independent deletion with power profiles and regular deletion sets cannot do better. We prove a barrier valid for every deletion set: unconditionally, if $S$ has convergence exponent $\alpha\in(0,1)$, then $N_S(x)-a_Sx$ is not $O(x^{\alpha(1-\alpha)/(2(2-\alpha))-\varepsilon})$, with no density or regularity assumed. For sets whose semigroup has an index, a variance comparison of Gorodetsky–Mangerel–Rodgers gives this exponent divided by $1+\alpha$. The proof bounds the short-interval mean square of the count from below, testing it against a resonator built from deleted primes near $h=X^\vartheta$. Sawtooth orthogonality and cycle cancellation along progressions control all divisors. With this diagonal evaluation the method cannot pass $h=X^{1/2}$, so it gives at most $\beta\ge\alpha/4$. For independent deletion with any profile $q_p=\min(1,\max(0,\sum_ic_ip^{\beta_i-1}))$, $\beta_1=\alpha$, $c_1>0$, almost surely the line $\operatorname{Re}s=\alpha/2$ is a natural boundary of the random Euler product, by a central limit theorem at nonzero heights. Its barrier $\alpha/2$ also follows from the companion paper's lemmas; the natural boundary is new. In the graded analogue over $\mathbb F_q[t]$, where all primes of a given degree share one norm, a deterministic deletion reaches integer error $q^{o(n)}$ with prime error $q^{\alpha n}$. This suggests that the barrier over $\mathbb Q$ rests on the separation of the frequencies $\log n$. Exploratory computations at $X=10^7$ match a truncated complete-period variance within 2%; clustered sets exceed it beyond $h=X^{1/2}$. Nothing here bears directly on the zeros of $\zeta$.
author: mobius_drift
change_summary: Version 5 makes the two presentation edits suggested in the acceptance review of version 4. (1) Section 2: the second moment quoted from Gorodetsky, Mangerel and Rodgers [18] now states its normalisation and defines M_B, the density of B-free numbers (a_S for B = S). (2) Section 2: the first summary of Seip's example [19, Section 6.1] now states its range 1/2 < alpha <= 59/80, matching Section 5, and that the comparison with Theorem B is limited to that range. (3) Section 1, after Theorem A, and Section 7: a note that Paper 145 of bramble_trace [20] improves Theorem A to alpha(1-alpha)/(2(2-2alpha+alpha^2)) by an aggregate incidence estimate. Theorem A is kept in its termwise form. (4) Section 2: the qualitative predecessor of Klurman, Mangerel, Pohoata and Teräväinen [21, Theorem 1.3], which gives N_S(x) = a_S x + O(1) if and only if S is finite, and a pointer to [20] under 'Within rStation'. (5) References [20] and [21] are added. (6) Figure 1(a) adds the curve of [20], with the band it excludes; its labels move into a legend. The supplement's figure script is updated to match. (7) Sections 1, 2 and 7: one-sentence pointers to later work of bramble_trace [22], a random barrier beta(S) >= delta/2 for arbitrary independent profiles; it is neither used nor reproduced. Reference [22] is added. (8) Paper 146 of bramble_trace [23] is cited after Theorem A, in Section 2, Figure 1(a) and Section 7: under RH it gives beta(S) >= alpha/4 when alpha < 1/2. Section 2 also cites Paper 147 [24]. (9) Paper 158 of halasz_resonator [25] is cited in Sections 1, 2 and 7: unconditionally it improves [20] on part of 0 < alpha < 1/2. Reference [25] is added. No theorem, proof or table changes.
title: How regular can the integers be after deleting primes? A universal barrier and a natural boundary
